We combine multi-stage cu rriculum learning, domain randomization, and a multi-scene updating strategy to address the conflicting challenges of obstacle avoidance and gate traversal. Our end-to-end control policy is implemented as a single network, allowing high-speed flight of quadrotors in environments with variable obstacles. Both hardware-in-the-loop and real-world experiments demonstrate that our method achieves faster lap times and higher success rates than existing approaches, effectively advancing drone racing in obstacle-rich environments. The video and code are available at: https://github.com/SJTU-ViSYS-team/CRL-Drone-Racing.

AI.tldr: Vision-based curriculum reinforcement learning framework for robust drone racing in obstacle-rich environments, achieving faster lap times and higher success rates than existing methods.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous drone racing research focuses primarily on obstacle-free racetracks, leaving perception and dynamic challenges of obstacles underexplored, resulting in low success rates and limited robustness in real-world flight.
AI.method: Novel vision-based curriculum reinforcement learning framework combining multi-stage curriculum learning, domain randomization, and multi-scene updating strategy to address conflicting challenges of obstacle avoidance and gate traversal. End-to-end control policy implemented as a single network.
AI.result: Both hardware-in-the-loop and real-world experiments demonstrate faster lap times and higher success rates than existing approaches, effectively advancing drone racing in obstacle-rich environments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables robust high-speed quadrotor flight in environments with variable obstacles, addressing previously underexplored challenges in autonomous drone racing.

title: Geometry-based pneumatic actuators for soft robotics
summary: Soft pneumatic actuators enable safe human-machine interaction with lightweight and powerful applied parts. On the other side, they suffer design limitations as regards complex actuation patterns, including minimum bending radii, multi-states capabilities and structural stability. We present geometry-based pneumatic actuators (GPAs), a design and implementation approach that introduces constraint layers with configurable CNC heat-sealed chambers. The approach achieves predictable deformation, near-zero bending radii, multi-states actuation, and enables customizable and repeatable complex actuated geometries. Mathematical modeling reveals predictable linear angle transformations and validates nonlinear torque-angle relationships across diverse configurations. We demonstrate versatility of the GPAs approach through three applications: a 49 g wrist exoskeleton reducing muscle activity by up to 51%, a 30.8 g haptic interface delivering 8 N force feedback with fast response, and a 208 g bipedal robot achieving multi-gait locomotion. GPAs establish a configurable platform for next-generation wearable robotics, haptic systems, and soft locomotion devices.

AI.tldr: Geometry-based pneumatic actuators (GPAs) use configurable CNC heat-sealed chambers to achieve predictable deformation, near-zero bending radii, multi-state actuation, and customizable complex geometries for wearable robotics, haptic interfaces, and soft locomotion.
AI.motivation: Soft pneumatic actuators enable safe human-machine interaction but suffer design limitations regarding complex actuation patterns, including minimum bending radii, multi-state capabilities, and structural stability.
AI.method: Introduces geometry-based pneumatic actuators (GPAs) with constraint layers featuring configurable CNC heat-sealed chambers, enabling predictable deformation and customizable geometries through mathematical modeling of linear angle transformations and nonlinear torque-angle relationships.
AI.result: Demonstrated versatility through three applications: 49 g wrist exoskeleton reducing muscle activity by up to 51%, 30.8 g haptic interface delivering 8 N force feedback with fast response, and 208 g bipedal robot achieving multi-gait locomotion.
AI.conclusion: GPAs establish a configurable platform for next-generation wearable robotics, haptic systems, and soft locomotion devices, overcoming traditional soft pneumatic actuator limitations.

title: Planning from Observation and Interaction
summary: Observational learning requires an agent to learn to perform a task by referencing only observations of the performed task. This work investigates the equivalent setting in real-world robot learning where access to hand-designed rewards and demonstrator actions are not assumed. To address this data-constrained setting, this work presents a planning-based Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) algorithm for world modeling from observation and interaction alone. Experiments conducted entirely in the real-world demonstrate that this paradigm is effective for learning image-based manipulation tasks from scratch in under an hour, without assuming prior knowledge, pre-training, or data of any kind beyond task observations. Moreover, this work demonstrates that the learned world model representation is capable of online transfer learning in the real-world from scratch. In comparison to existing approaches, including IRL, RL, and Behavior Cloning (BC), which have more restrictive assumptions, the proposed approach demonstrates significantly greater sample efficiency and success rates, enabling a practical path forward for online world modeling and planning from observation and interaction. Videos and more at: https://uwrobotlearning.github.io/mpail2/.

AI.tldr: Proposes a planning-based IRL algorithm for real-world robot learning from observation alone, enabling image-based manipulation learning in under an hour without rewards, demonstrator actions, or prior data.
AI.motivation: Addresses the challenge of observational learning in real-world robotics where access to hand-designed rewards and demonstrator actions is not available, aiming to enable practical robot learning from observation and interaction alone.
AI.method: Develops a planning-based Inverse Reinforcement Learning algorithm for world modeling that learns from observation and interaction without requiring rewards, demonstrator actions, or prior knowledge.
AI.result: Demonstrates effective learning of image-based manipulation tasks from scratch in under an hour in real-world experiments, with the learned world model supporting online transfer learning and outperforming existing IRL, RL, and BC approaches in sample efficiency and success rates.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides a practical path forward for online world modeling and planning from observation and interaction, overcoming restrictive assumptions of existing methods and enabling efficient real-world robot learning.

title: Robust Skills, Brittle Grounding: Diagnosing Restricted Generalization in Vision-Language Action Policies via Multi-Object Picking
summary: Vision-language action (VLA) policies often report strong manipulation benchmark performance with relatively few demonstrations, but it remains unclear whether this reflects robust language-to-object grounding or reliance on object--location correlations that do not transfer beyond the training distribution. We present a controlled multi-object picking study that progressively increases object placement variability up to full workspace randomization and evaluates held-out object--location pairings that break familiar associations without increasing spatial difficulty. Across these stress tests and data scaling, we find that for representative VLA policies, including SmolVLA and $π_{0.5}$, execution of the manipulation primitive remains substantially more reliable than instruction-conditioned task success in harder regimes, suggesting that manipulation skill acquisition is decoupled from instruction following. We recommend augmenting manipulation benchmarks with task ladders and decomposed metrics that separately measure primitive execution and instruction-conditioned success to better diagnose instruction-grounded generalization.

AI.tldr: VLA policies show strong benchmark performance but may rely on object-location correlations rather than robust language grounding; controlled experiments reveal manipulation primitives remain reliable while instruction-conditioned success fails under object placement variability.
AI.motivation: To determine whether vision-language action policies achieve strong manipulation performance through robust language-to-object grounding or by exploiting object-location correlations that don't generalize beyond training distributions.
AI.method: Conducted controlled multi-object picking study with progressive workspace randomization, evaluating held-out object-location pairings that break familiar associations without increasing spatial difficulty. Tested representative VLA policies (SmolVLA and π₀.₅) across stress tests and data scaling.
AI.result: Manipulation primitive execution remains substantially more reliable than instruction-conditioned task success in harder regimes, suggesting manipulation skill acquisition is decoupled from instruction following. Policies struggle with instruction-grounded generalization when object-location correlations are broken.
AI.conclusion: Manipulation benchmarks should be augmented with task ladders and decomposed metrics that separately measure primitive execution and instruction-conditioned success to better diagnose instruction-grounded generalization in VLA policies.

title: SafeGen-LLM: Enhancing Safety Generalization in Task Planning for Robotic Systems
summary: Safety-critical task planning in robotic systems remains challenging: classical planners suffer from poor scalability, Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based methods generalize poorly, and base Large Language Models (LLMs) cannot guarantee safety. To address this gap, we propose safety-generalizable large language models, named SafeGen-LLM. SafeGen-LLM can not only enhance the safety satisfaction of task plans but also generalize well to novel safety properties in various domains. We first construct a multi-domain Planning Domain Definition Language 3 (PDDL3) benchmark with explicit safety constraints. Then, we introduce a two-stage post-training framework: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on a constraint-compliant planning dataset to learn planning syntax and semantics, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) guided by fine-grained reward machines derived from formal verification to enforce safety alignment and by curriculum learning to better handle complex tasks. Extensive experiments show that SafeGen-LLM achieves strong safety generalization and outperforms frontier proprietary baselines across multi-domain planning tasks and multiple input formats (e.g., PDDLs and natural language).

AI.tldr: SafeGen-LLM is a safety-generalizable LLM for robotic task planning that combines SFT and GRPO training to ensure safety compliance and generalization across domains.
AI.motivation: Classical planners have scalability issues, RL methods generalize poorly, and base LLMs cannot guarantee safety in safety-critical robotic task planning.
AI.method: Two-stage post-training: 1) SFT on constraint-compliant planning dataset to learn planning syntax/semantics; 2) GRPO guided by fine-grained reward machines from formal verification for safety alignment, plus curriculum learning for complex tasks.
AI.result: SafeGen-LLM achieves strong safety generalization and outperforms frontier proprietary baselines across multi-domain planning tasks with multiple input formats (PDDLs and natural language).
AI.conclusion: SafeGen-LLM addresses the safety generalization gap in robotic task planning by combining formal verification with LLM training, enabling safe planning across novel safety properties and domains.

title: Humanoid Robots as First Assistants in Endoscopic Surgery
summary: Humanoid robots have become a focal point of technological ambition, with claims of surgical capability within years in mainstream discourse. These projections are aspirational yet lack empirical grounding. To date, no humanoid has assisted a surgeon through an actual procedure, let alone performed one. The work described here breaks this new ground. Here we report a proof of concept in which a teleoperated Unitree G1 provided endoscopic visualization while an attending otolaryngologist performed a cadaveric sphenoidectomy. The procedure was completed successfully, with stable visualization maintained throughout. Teleoperation allowed assessment of whether the humanoid form factor could meet the physical demands of surgical assistance in terms of sustenance and precision; the cognitive demands were satisfied -- for now -- by the operator. Post-procedure analysis identified engineering targets for clinical translation, alongside near-term opportunities such as autonomous diagnostic scoping. This work establishes form-factor feasibility for humanoid surgical assistance while identifying challenges for continued development.

AI.tldr: First demonstration of a humanoid robot (Unitree G1) providing endoscopic visualization assistance during a cadaveric surgical procedure, establishing form-factor feasibility for humanoid surgical assistance.
AI.motivation: To provide empirical grounding for claims about humanoid surgical capabilities by demonstrating actual surgical assistance, as no humanoid has previously assisted in real surgical procedures despite optimistic projections.
AI.method: Teleoperated Unitree G1 humanoid robot provided endoscopic visualization while an attending otolaryngologist performed a cadaveric sphenoidectomy. The setup tested physical demands (sustenance and precision) of the humanoid form factor for surgical assistance.
AI.result: Procedure completed successfully with stable visualization maintained throughout. Post-procedure analysis identified engineering targets for clinical translation and near-term opportunities like autonomous diagnostic scoping.
AI.conclusion: Establishes form-factor feasibility for humanoid surgical assistance while identifying challenges for continued development. Demonstrates that humanoid robots can meet physical demands of surgical assistance, though cognitive demands currently require human operators.

title: How IMU Drift Influences Multi-Radar Inertial Odometry for Ground Robots in Subterranean Terrains
comment: Accepted in IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), 2026
summary: Reliable radar inertial odometry (RIO) requires mitigating IMU bias drift, a challenge that intensifies in subterranean environments due to extreme temperatures and gravity-induced accelerations. Cost-effective IMUs such as the Pixhawk, when paired with FMCW TI IWR6843AOP EVM radars, suffer from drift-induced degradation compounded by sparse, noisy, and flickering radar returns, making fusion less stable than LiDAR-based odometry. Yet, LiDAR fails under smoke, dust, and aerosols, whereas FMCW radars remain compact, lightweight, cost-effective, and robust in these situations. To address these challenges, we propose a two-stage MRIO framework that combines an IMU bias estimator for resilient localization and mapping in GPS-denied subterranean environments affected by smoke. Radar-based ego-velocity estimation is formulated through a least-squares approach and incorporated into an EKF for online IMU bias correction; the corrected IMU accelerations are fused with heterogeneous measurements from multiple radars and an IMU to refine odometry. The proposed framework further supports radar-only mapping by exploiting the robot's estimated translational and rotational displacements. In subterranean field trials, MRIO delivers robust localization and mapping, outperforming EKF-RIO. It maintains accuracy across cost-efficient FMCW radar setups and different IMUs, showing resilience with Pixhawk and higher-grade units such as VectorNav. The implementation will be provided as an open-source resource to the community (code available at https://github.com/LTU-RAI/MRIO

AI.tldr: MRIO is a two-stage radar-inertial odometry framework that addresses IMU bias drift in GPS-denied subterranean environments, using online IMU bias correction via EKF with radar ego-velocity estimation and supporting radar-only mapping.
AI.motivation: Cost-effective IMUs like Pixhawk suffer from bias drift in extreme subterranean conditions, while radar returns are sparse and noisy. LiDAR fails under smoke/dust, but FMCW radars remain robust. Need resilient localization/mapping in GPS-denied, smoke-affected subterranean environments.
AI.method: Two-stage MRIO framework: 1) IMU bias estimator using radar-based ego-velocity estimation via least-squares approach, incorporated into EKF for online IMU bias correction. 2) Corrected IMU accelerations fused with heterogeneous measurements from multiple radars and IMU to refine odometry. Supports radar-only mapping using estimated translational/rotational displacements.
AI.result: In subterranean field trials, MRIO delivers robust localization and mapping, outperforming EKF-RIO. Maintains accuracy across cost-efficient FMCW radar setups and different IMUs (Pixhawk and higher-grade VectorNav). Shows resilience in challenging conditions.
AI.conclusion: MRIO provides effective solution for IMU bias drift in subterranean environments, enabling robust radar-inertial odometry that works with cost-effective hardware. Framework supports radar-only mapping and will be open-sourced to community.

title: Evaluating Accuracy of Vine Robot Shape Sensing with Distributed Inertial Measurement Units
summary: Soft, tip-extending vine robots are well suited for navigating tight, debris-filled environments, making them ideal for urban search and rescue. Sensing the full shape of a vine robot's body is helpful both for localizing information from other sensors placed along the robot body and for determining the robot's configuration within the space being explored. Prior approaches have localized vine robot tips using a single inertial measurement unit (IMU) combined with force sensing or length estimation, while one method demonstrated full-body shape sensing using distributed IMUs on a passively steered robot in controlled maze environments. However, the accuracy of distributed IMU-based shape sensing under active steering, varying robot lengths, and different sensor spacings has not been systematically quantified. In this work, we experimentally evaluate the accuracy of vine robot shape sensing using distributed IMUs along the robot body. We quantify IMU drift, measuring an average orientation drift rate of 1.33 degrees/min across 15 sensors. For passive steering, mean tip position error was 11% of robot length. For active steering, mean tip position error increased to 16%. During growth experiments across lengths from 30-175 cm, mean tip error was 8%, with a positive trend with increasing length. We also analyze the influence of sensor spacing and observe that intermediate spacings can minimize error for single-curvature shapes. These results demonstrate the feasibility of distributed IMU-based shape sensing for vine robots while highlighting key limitations and opportunities for improved modeling and algorithmic integration for field deployment.

AI.tldr: Experimental evaluation of distributed IMU-based shape sensing for vine robots, quantifying accuracy under passive/active steering, varying lengths, and sensor spacing effects.
AI.motivation: Vine robots need full-body shape sensing for sensor localization and configuration determination in search/rescue applications. Prior work used single IMUs or distributed IMUs in controlled settings, but accuracy under active steering, varying lengths, and different sensor spacings hasn't been systematically quantified.
AI.method: Experimental evaluation using distributed IMUs along vine robot body. Quantified IMU drift rates, measured shape sensing accuracy for passive/active steering, tested across lengths (30-175 cm), and analyzed sensor spacing effects.
AI.result: Average IMU orientation drift: 1.33°/min. Passive steering: mean tip position error 11% of robot length. Active steering: mean error increased to 16%. Growth experiments: mean tip error 8% with positive trend with length. Intermediate sensor spacings minimize error for single-curvature shapes.
AI.conclusion: Distributed IMU-based shape sensing is feasible for vine robots but has limitations. Results highlight opportunities for improved modeling and algorithmic integration for field deployment, particularly addressing drift, active steering challenges, and optimal sensor spacing.
